title: Laudato Si' (2015)
hookLine: Francis writes on care for our common home

lines: A SAINT'S SONG, A POPE'S LETTER.
cards: "Laudato si', mi' Signore." Praised be you, my Lord.
That's a line from a song Francis of Assisi wrote, in his own Italian dialect, praising God through Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, and, as he puts it, our sister, Mother Earth.
Centuries later, a pope who took Francis's name borrowed that line for the title of a letter. Not about prayer, exactly. About rivers, air, soil, the poor, and the way they're tied together.
He addressed it not only to Catholics but to everyone living on the planet, with a subtitle: on care for our common home.

teach.h: PART OF NATURE, INCLUDED IN IT.
teach.b: Francis calls the idea integral ecology. Integral means whole, nothing left out. First, the whole includes us.

Ecology can sound like nature over there: forests, whales, glaciers. Francis says people are part of nature, included in it, not looking at it from outside, and what they do to it they do to themselves and to each other.
Second, the crises are one crisis.

teach.h: ONE CRISIS, BOTH SOCIAL AND NATURAL.
teach.b: There aren't two separate problems, one environmental and one social, but a single, complex crisis that is both. Polluted water and poverty, he says, often land on the same people.
So caring for the earth and caring for the poor can't be split into separate departments. Third, the root is in the heart. He talks about habits: buying without thinking, using things up, rushing.
He calls for an ecological conversion, a change of heart that shows up in small daily acts, like turning off unneeded lights, using less plastic, cooking only what will be eaten.
Fourth, it starts in praise. Before it's a duty, it's wonder.
This path met the verse back in year one, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Very good, before anyone had used them for anything.
Francis keeps returning to a phrase that sums it up, today's line: everything is connected. A choice at a grocery store, a factory far away, a family's water, a bird's nest, God's delight. One web.

how: Catholic parishes and schools read Laudato Si' in study groups, some keep a Season of Creation in early autumn, and some form care-for-creation teams that work on energy, waste and local gardens.

o: a pledge to plant a new tree every year
the science of how forests and oceans work
seeing the earth, the poor and our habits as one

p: a change of heart in daily habits

games.q: you lead a parish. one group wants to help the poor; another wants to protect a local river. how does Laudato Si' see it?
o: pick one; the poor come first.
pick one; the river comes first.
games.why: Francis argues the two crises are one, and that polluted water and poverty often land on the same people. everything is connected.

practice: Go to a door or a window, or out onto a step; if you can't, close your eyes and remember the last time you stood outdoors.
Notice one living thing, a tree, a weed in a crack, a bird, the sky itself, long enough to see something you missed, then follow one thread: the water it needs, the air you share with it.
If you pray, say Francis of Assisi's line, praised be you, my Lord; if you don't, simply let yourself be glad it's there.

wordCard.voice: Integral ecology. The whole picture: the earth, the poor, our habits and our praise, held together as one. Today's word.

orig.note: Not Latin: the Umbrian Italian of Francis of Assisi's song, praised be you, my Lord.

carryVoice: Your line: everything is connected. One web, and you're inside it. Until tomorrow.
